chapter_summary:
Having a backup is only half the battle; being able to successfully restore it is the ultimate goal. Logical backups, created with `pg_dump` and `pg_dumpall`, are restored using either the `psql` command-line client or the `pg_restore` utility, depending on the backup format. Understanding which tool to use and its various options is crucial for a smooth recovery process.

For plain-text SQL backups (created with `pg_dump -F p` or `pg_dumpall`), the `psql` command-line client is your go-to tool. This is essentially executing the SQL script generated by `pg_dump` or `pg_dumpall`.
To restore a `pg_dumpall` backup, which contains global objects and all databases, you typically run it against the `postgres` database (or any other existing database) as a superuser. It's often recommended to stop applications and ensure no other connections are active during a full cluster restore.
```bash
psql -U postgres -f /tmp/full_cluster_global.sql postgres
```
This command connects to the `postgres` database as the `postgres` user and executes the SQL commands from `full_cluster_global.sql`. This script will create roles, tablespaces, and then each database, before populating them.

To restore a plain-text `pg_dump` backup of a single database, you first need to create an empty database, then connect to it with `psql` and execute the script:
```bash
# First, create the empty database (if it doesn't exist or you want to overwrite)
# If the backup file itself contains CREATE DATABASE, you can skip this and use --create with psql
createdb -U postgres mydatabase_restored

# Then, restore the data
psql -U postgres -d mydatabase_restored -f /tmp/mydatabase_backup.sql
```
A common mistake here is trying to restore a `pg_dump` plain text file into an existing database that already has the tables. This will result in errors like "table already exists." To avoid this, you can either drop the database first (`dropdb mydatabase_restored`) or ensure your `pg_dump` included the `--clean` option, which adds `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` statements to the backup script.

For custom (`-F c`), tar (`-F t`), and directory (`-F d`) format backups, you *must* use the `pg_restore` utility. `pg_restore` is much more powerful than `psql` for these formats, offering options for selective restoration, parallel processing, and more.
To perform a full restore from a custom format backup:
```bash
# First, create the empty database
createdb -U postgres mydatabase_restored

# Then, restore using pg_restore
pg_restore -U postgres -d mydatabase_restored /tmp/mydatabase_backup.custom
```
The `--clean` option for `pg_restore` will drop existing objects before recreating them, which is useful when restoring to an existing database. The `--create` option will attempt to create the database before restoring, so you wouldn't need `createdb` separately.
```bash
# Restore, dropping existing objects and creating the database if necessary
pg_restore -U postgres --clean --create -d mydatabase_restored /tmp/mydatabase_backup.custom
```
One of the most powerful features of `pg_restore` with custom or directory format backups is **selective restoration**. You can choose to restore only specific tables, schemas, or other objects.
To restore only a specific table (e.g., `products` table) from a custom backup:
```bash
pg_restore -U postgres -d mydatabase_restored --table=products /tmp/mydatabase_backup.custom
```
To restore only a specific schema (e.g., `public` schema):
```bash
pg_restore -U postgres -d mydatabase_restored --schema=public /tmp/mydatabase_backup.custom
```
You can also list the contents of a custom or tar backup file without restoring it, which is incredibly useful for verifying its contents or planning a selective restore:
```bash
pg_restore -l /tmp/mydatabase_backup.custom
```
This will output a list of all objects contained within the backup file, each with an ID that can be used with the `--use-list` option for very fine-grained selective restoration.

For very large databases, `pg_restore` supports parallel restoration using the `--jobs=N` option (where `N` is the number of parallel jobs). This can significantly speed up the restore process, especially when restoring to a powerful server.
```bash
pg_restore -U postgres -d mydatabase_restored --jobs=4 /tmp/mydatabase_backup.custom
```
When restoring, always ensure the target database server has sufficient resources (CPU, RAM, disk I/O). A common mistake during restoration is insufficient disk space on the target server. Another is permission issues: ensure the PostgreSQL user performing the restore has the necessary privileges to create databases, tables, and insert data. Before any critical restore operation, it's a best practice to test the restore process on a non-production environment. This validates the integrity of your backup files and familiarizes you with the steps involved, reducing stress and potential errors during an actual disaster.

screens.title: Restoring Logical Backups
screens.subtitle: Using psql and pg_restore to recover databases, selectively or in full

narration.text: Restoring a logical backup is the moment your planning earns real value. In this lesson we focus on the two tools you will use: the psql client for plain-text S Q L dumps and pg_restore for custom, tar, and directory-format backups. You will learn practical, repeatable steps: when to create an empty database first, how to use --clean and --create safely, and how to extract just the objects you need with --table or --schema. The chapter includes terminal-ready commands you can copy into a lab, plus verification queries to confirm success. We will also highlight common pitfalls such as restoring into a database that already contains objects, missing disk space, or insufficient privileges, and show how a test restore removes uncertainty before a production recovery. By the end, you will understand which tool to choose and why selective restores can save time during emergencies. Think of this chapter as a short operations playbook: follow the steps, verify your data counts, and you will reduce downtime and surprises.

keyIdea.text: Choose psql for plain-text SQL backups and pg_restore for custom/tar/directory formats; use --clean and --create to control object recreation and enable selective restores when needed.

screens.title: Which tool to use: psql vs pg_restore
screens.subtitle: Decide by backup format and required capabilities

narration.text: Choosing the right tool starts with the backup format. Plain-text S Q L dumps produced by pg_dump -F p or pg_dumpall are executed as S Q L scripts, so you use the psql client to run them. This is effectively replaying the S Q L commands that create roles, tablespaces, schemas, and data. In contrast, custom, tar, or directory-format backups require pg_restore. These are archive formats that store object metadata separately and allow selective extraction, parallel replays, and listing of contained objects. A common misconception is that psql can always restore any file; it cannot handle archive formats created by pg_dump with -F c, -F t, or -F d. Another useful distinction: psql will reflect exactly the S Q L as generated, including DROP statements if --clean was used when dumping; pg_restore reconstructs objects and optionally issues drops if you pass --clean. Concrete example: to restore a plain-text dump you might run psql -U postgres -f /tmp/mydb. sql mydb_restore after creating the database; for a custom archive, you run pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb_restore /tmp/mydb. custom. Always verify with quick queries after the restore. Which format are your backups in, and which tool does that imply?

keyIdea.title: Tool selection
keyIdea.text: Use psql for plain-text SQL dumps; use pg_restore for custom, tar, and directory archive formats because it supports selective and parallel restores.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Which tool to use
Definition

psql and pg_restore: what they do

psql executes plain SQL scripts. pg_restore reads archive formats and reconstructs objects selectively or in parallel.

When to use psql
Plain-text dumps from pg_dump or pg_dumpall; you replay SQL statements directly.
When to use pg_restore
Custom, tar, or directory format backups created with -F c, -F t, or -F d.
Key Takeaway

Match tool to backup format: psql for SQL scripts, pg_restore for archives with selective and parallel features.

Terminal examples
createdb -U postgres mydb_restore psql -U postgres -d mydb_restore -f /tmp/mydb_dump.sql # For archive formats createdb -U postgres mydb_restore pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb_restore /tmp/mydb.custom
Common misconception
psql cannot unpack custom/tar/directory archive formats; those require pg_restore.
Check your backup format
If unsure, try pg_restore -l on the file. If it lists objects, use pg_restore; otherwise, psql can run the SQL file.

screens.title: Restoring plain-text SQL with psql
screens.subtitle: Create or reuse a database, then execute the SQL script

narration.text: Restoring a plain-text S Q L dump is a straightforward process, but the sequence matters. First, decide whether the dump contains a CREATE DATABASE statement. If it does, you can use psql to run the script directly against an existing database like postgres; otherwise create an empty target database with createdb. Next, confirm there are no active connections that might conflict with schema creation. Then run psql -U postgres -d target_db -f /path/to/backup. sql to execute the script. A frequent error is attempting to restore into an existing database that already contains tables from the same names; this leads to 'table already exists' errors. To avoid this, either drop and recreate the database before restoring or ensure the dump includes DROP statements by using --clean at dump time. After the restore finishes, run verification queries such as SELECT COUNT(*) FROM important_table; and list tables with \dt to confirm objects are present. Always test this sequence on a non-production server first so you can practice recovery without risking live data. Restoring plain-text SQL with psql means confirm whether the dump creates the database, create an empty database if needed, then use psql -f to execute the sql script and verify with row counts.. In practical terms, create or reuse a database, then execute the sql script. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Plain-text restore flow
keyIdea.text: Confirm whether the dump creates the database, create an empty database if needed, then use psql -f to execute the SQL script and verify with row counts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Plain-text restore
Steps
  1. Check whether the dump contains CREATE DATABASE. If not, run createdb -U postgres target_db.
  2. Stop applications or disconnect clients to avoid conflicts during schema creation.
  3. Run psql -U postgres -d target_db -f /tmp/backup.sql and monitor for errors.
  4. Verify using SELECT COUNT(*) and \dt to inspect tables and row counts.
Common mistake

Restoring into a database that already has tables will produce 'table already exists'. Drop-and-create or use --clean at dump time to prevent this.

Terminal: example sequence
# Create an empty database createdb -U postgres sales_db_restore_plain # Restore the plain-text SQL dump psql -U postgres -d sales_db_restore_plain -f /tmp/sales_db_plain.sql # Verify a table count psql -U postgres -d sales_db_restore_plain -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products;"
Scenario
Use this flow when your backup is a plain SQL file created without archive options.

screens.title: Restoring global objects from pg_dumpall
screens.subtitle: Roles, tablespaces, and cluster-wide SQL executed as a superuser

narration.text: pg_dumpall produces a plain-text script that includes global objects like roles and tablespaces along with the S Q L to create each database. Restoring such a dump is different from restoring a single database: you typically run the global script against an existing maintenance database such as postgres while connected as a superuser. Before running a cluster restore, stop applications and ensure no conflicting sessions exist so role creation succeeds. The command is straightforward: psql -U postgres -f /tmp/full_cluster_global. sql postgres. The script will create roles and tablespaces first, then create and populate each database. A common misconception is that a full cluster restore can be applied piecemeal; global objects must be restored in the cluster context. After the restore, verify that roles exist and that databases are present. If your environment requires finer control, extract parts of the dump or test the full script on a staging server first to confirm it behaves as expected. Restoring global objects from pg_dumpall means use psql to execute pg_dumpall's global sql as a superuser against an existing database to recreate roles, tablespaces, and all databases.. In practical terms, roles, tablespaces, and cluster-wide sql executed as a superuser. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cluster restore behavior
keyIdea.text: Use psql to execute pg_dumpall's global SQL as a superuser against an existing database to recreate roles, tablespaces, and all databases.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Global restore
Definition

A pg_dumpall global dump contains cluster-level SQL for roles, tablespaces, and the CREATE DATABASE statements for every database in the cluster.

Recommended command
psql -U postgres -f /tmp/full_cluster_global.sql postgres
Why stop applications first?
Active sessions can block role creation or interfere with tablespace operations, causing the restore to fail or be inconsistent.
Verification
After the script runs, confirm global state and one sample database.
# List roles psql -U postgres -d postgres -c "\du" # Check a restored database psql -U postgres -d example_db -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products;"
Misconception check
Global restore is not limited to single-database objects. Roles and tablespaces must be applied in the cluster context before restoring individual databases.

screens.title: Using pg_restore for custom, tar, and directory formats
screens.subtitle: Full restores when backups are in archive formats

narration.text: pg_restore is the tool you must use for custom, tar, and directory-format backups created by pg_dump with -F c, -F t, or -F d. These formats are archive-like and keep object metadata separate from raw S Q L, enabling flexible restoration strategies. The typical full-restore flow is: create an empty database with createdb, then run pg_restore -U postgres -d mydatabase_restore /path/to/backup. custom. If your backup contains the CREATE DATABASE statement, consider using pg_restore --create so the utility handles database creation for you. pg_restore supports many options: --clean to drop objects before recreating them, --schema and --table to restrict what you restore, and --jobs for parallel execution. A common mistake is attempting to use psql on an archive file; pg_restore will report unreadable contents. After pg_restore completes, verify restored objects with \dt and run sample queries. Keep in mind permissions: the restoring user needs privileges to create objects, and the server must have sufficient disk space and resources for any parallel jobs. Using pg_restore for custom, tar, and directory formats means use pg_restore to rebuild databases from archive formats; it offers options for clean restores, selective object restores, and parallel jobs.. In practical terms, full restores when backups are in archive formats. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: pg_restore basics
keyIdea.text: Use pg_restore to rebuild databases from archive formats; it offers options for clean restores, selective object restores, and parallel jobs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › pg_restore basics
Full restore example
# Create database createdb -U postgres sales_db_restore # Restore from custom format pg_restore -U postgres -d sales_db_restore /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump # Or let pg_restore create the DB pg_restore -U postgres --clean --create -d sales_db_restore /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump
When to use --create
Use --create when the archive includes a CREATE DATABASE entry and you want pg_restore to handle creation for you.
Options at a glance
  • --clean: drop objects before recreating them to avoid conflicts.
  • --create: create the database from the archive's metadata.
  • --table/--schema: restrict restoration to specific objects.
  • --jobs=N: run parallel workers to speed up restore.
Misconception
Using --create with an existing database name may not drop the prior database. Understand whether you need to drop first or rely on pg_restore's options.

screens.title: --clean and --create options
screens.subtitle: How they change restore behavior and when to use them

narration.text: The --clean and --create options control whether existing objects are removed and whether the target database is created during a restore. --clean tells pg_restore to issue DROP statements before recreating each object, which avoids 'table already exists' errors when restoring into an existing database. This is useful when you want the archive to overwrite conflicting objects without manually dropping everything. --create instructs pg_restore to create the database from the archive metadata, which simplifies the workflow by combining createdb and restore into one step. A common pitfall is assuming --create will force-drop an existing database; it does not necessarily drop and recreate the database itself unless the archive includes a drop or you combine it with external drop commands. Practical example: to both drop objects and create the database, you can run pg_restore --clean --create -d target_db backup. custom. Always confirm privileges: the restoring user must be able to drop and create databases, and you should test on a non-production server to avoid accidental data loss. --clean and --create options means --clean drops objects before recreation; --create makes pg_restore create the database from the archive metadata. use both carefully in production.. In practical terms, how they change restore behavior and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Control options
keyIdea.text: --clean drops objects before recreation; --create makes pg_restore create the database from the archive metadata. Use both carefully in production.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › --clean and --create
Option: --clean

When you pass --clean, pg_restore drops objects it will recreate. This prevents conflicts but requires appropriate privileges.

Example: pg_restore -U postgres --clean -d mydb /tmp/mybackup.custom
Warning
--clean will remove objects. Ensure you don't accidentally delete data you need.
Option: --create

--create tells pg_restore to create the database before restoring its contents, using the archive's metadata when available.

Example: pg_restore -U postgres --create -d mydb /tmp/mybackup.custom
Pro tip
Combine --clean and --create to drop existing objects and create the database if the archive includes creation metadata.

screens.title: Selective restoration with pg_restore (--table / --schema)
screens.subtitle: Restore only the objects you need to minimize impact

narration.text: One of the most practical features of pg_restore is selective restoration. When a full restore is unnecessary or risky, you can extract only specific tables or schemas using --table or --schema. For example, to restore only the products table you would run pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb --table=products /tmp/mydb_backup. custom after creating an empty target database. Selective restores are invaluable when a single table is corrupted or when you need to move a subset of data for testing. A common misconception is that selective restores always include dependent objects automatically; pg_restore restores the requested object but may not include related objects unless you also select them or use a list file. If you need fine-grained control, use pg_restore -l to list object IDs, edit the list to include precisely what you want, and then supply it with --use-list. After restoring, verify the object with \dt and a row count. This workflow reduces downtime and avoids unnecessary data movement during recovery. Selective restoration with pg_restore (--table / --schema) means use --table or --schema to restore only required objects. for very fine control, list archive contents with pg_restore -l and use --use-list.. In practical terms, restore only the objects you need to minimize impact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Selective restores
keyIdea.text: Use --table or --schema to restore only required objects. For very fine control, list archive contents with pg_restore -l and use --use-list.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Selective restoration
Quick example
# Create database createdb -U postgres sales_db_restore_selective # Restore only the products table pg_restore -U postgres -d sales_db_restore_selective --table=products /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump # Verify psql -U postgres -d sales_db_restore_selective -c "\dt" psql -U postgres -d sales_db_restore_selective -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products;"
When to use
Recover a single corrupted table, or move only the data needed for a patch or test environment.
Use the contents list
For fine-grained control, list archive contents and build a use-list that pg_restore can apply.
pg_restore -l /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump
Misconception
Restoring a table alone may miss dependent objects. Check and include constraints, indexes, and related sequences if needed.

screens.title: Listing backup contents and using --use-list
screens.subtitle: Inspect archives before restoring to plan selective restores

narration.text: Before performing a selective restore, inspect the archive contents with pg_restore -l. This command outputs a list of the objects stored in the archive along with item IDs that you can use to build a precise restoration plan. Listing is especially helpful for complex backups containing many schemas, tables, and custom types. Once you have the list, you can edit it to include only the items you want restored, and then feed it back to pg_restore with --use-list to apply that exact subset. A practical example: run pg_restore -l /tmp/mybackup. custom > content. list, open content. list, remove lines for objects you do not want, then run pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb --use-list=content. list /tmp/mybackup. custom. A common misconception is that --table or --schema will always be simpler; for very fine-grained control or when restoring by object ID, a list is the most deterministic approach. Always test your use-list on a staging server to ensure you captured the correct dependencies before applying it to production. Listing backup contents and using --use-list means use pg_restore -l to list archive contents and --use-list with an edited list file to restore precisely the objects you want.. In practical terms, inspect archives before restoring to plan selective restores. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inspect before restoring
keyIdea.text: Use pg_restore -l to list archive contents and --use-list with an edited list file to restore precisely the objects you want.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Listing archive contents
List the archive
pg_restore -l /tmp/mybackup.custom > content.list # Edit content.list to keep only the IDs you want # Then restore using the edited list pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb --use-list=content.list /tmp/mybackup.custom
Why use a list
A list gives deterministic control over exactly which objects are restored, including object IDs and order.
Best practice

Always test your edited list on staging. Confirm dependent objects such as constraints and sequences are included or restored separately if needed.

Misconception
A list doesn't automatically resolve object dependencies for you. Verify and include related objects manually when necessary.

screens.title: Parallel restoration with --jobs
screens.subtitle: Speed up large restores while watching resource limits

narration.text: For very large backups, pg_restore can run parallel workers with the --jobs option to speed up restore time. Specify --jobs=N where N is the number of worker processes. Parallel restores work well when the archive contains many separate table restores that can run concurrently. However, parallel workers increase C P U, memory, and input and output demands on the target server, so choose N based on available resources and test performance. Example: pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb_restore --jobs=4 /tmp/mybackup. custom. A common mistake is setting N too high and saturating disk input and output, causing the restore to become slower or fail. Also, parallel restore requires archive formats that support it (custom or directory); plain S Q L and tar formats may have limitations. After a parallel restore, run verification queries and inspect logs for worker errors. Use --jobs in a staged test environment first to tune the right level for your infrastructure. keyIdea.title: Parallel restores
keyIdea.text: Use --jobs to run parallel worker processes for faster restores, but match the job count to server CPU, memory, and I/O capacity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Parallel restoration
Example command
pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb_restore --jobs=4 /tmp/mybackup.custom
When it helps
Large backups with many independent table restores; a multi-core, high-I/O server.
Risks and tuning
  • Monitor disk I/O and CPU to avoid saturation.
  • Test different job counts in staging to find optimal N.
  • Not all archive formats or operations parallelize equally.
Misconception
Higher job counts always equal faster restores. In practice, I/O or lock contention can become the bottleneck.

screens.title: Verification and common troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Checks and fixes after a logical restore

narration.text: Verification is the final, essential step after any restore. Run simple checks like \dt to list tables, SELECT COUNT(*) FROM key_table to confirm expected row counts, and inspect roles with \du. Common issues include insufficient disk space, causing incomplete restores; permission errors when the restoring user lacks create or drop rights; and object conflicts when restoring into a non-empty database. A frequent troubleshooting pattern is to read the restore output for the first error, fix that underlying environmental cause, and then either re-run the restore or perform a targeted restore of remaining objects. When permission issues arise, ensure the postgres user or the role you use has the required privileges. For disk space, confirm the server has room for the restored data and temporary files. Always rehearse restores on a staging server and document the sequence, including any prerequisite roles or tablespaces, so a production restore goes smoothly under pressure. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Verification & troubleshooting
Quick verification
psql -U postgres -d mydb -c "\dt" psql -U postgres -d mydb -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products;" psql -U postgres -d postgres -c "\du"
Key Takeaway
Verification queries are quick and provide confidence that restores succeeded.
Common errors & fixes
  • table already exists → use --clean or drop/recreate database
  • permission denied → ensure restoring role has create/drop privileges
  • out of disk space → provision more disk and retry
Pro tip
Always run a full test restore on a staging server before a production recovery to exercise the entire workflow and detect environmental gaps.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: restore scenarios
screens.subtitle: Practice full, custom, and selective restores with verification

narration.text: This activity walks through four practical restore scenarios you can run in a lab. Scenario one is a full plain-text restore: drop or create an empty database, then run psql -f to replay the S Q L and verify with SELECT COUNT(*). Scenario two uses pg_restore with --clean and --create to let pg_restore create the database and drop conflicting objects. Scenario three demonstrates selective restoration: create an empty database and restore only the products table with --table=products. Scenario four shows listing archive contents with pg_restore -l so you can edit and use a precise object list. For each scenario run the verification queries shown in the earlier screens. A common learner mistake is skipping verification or not confirming privileges; always ensure the postgres user you run commands with has the permissions needed. After completing the scenarios, reflect on when a selective restore saved time versus when a full restore was more appropriate. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Hands-on activity
Activity steps
Scenario 1: Plain-text full restore
dropdb -U postgres sales_db createdb -U postgres sales_db_restore_plain psql -U postgres -d sales_db_restore_plain -f /tmp/sales_db_plain.sql Verify: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products;
Scenario 2: Custom format with --clean/--create
pg_restore -U postgres --clean --create -d sales_db_restore_custom /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump Verify: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers;
Scenario 3: Selective table restore
createdb -U postgres sales_db_restore_selective pg_restore -U postgres -d sales_db_restore_selective --table=products /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump Verify: \dt and SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products;
Scenario 4: List and use-list
pg_restore -l /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump > mylist.txt Edit mylist.txt to include IDs you want, then: pg_restore -U postgres -d mydb --use-list=mylist.txt /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump
Verification checklist
  • Confirm tables exist (\dt)
  • Run row counts on key tables
  • Check roles and tablespaces
Reflection
When did a selective restore save time? When did a full restore make more sense? Note your answers for later discussion.

These three points form the foundation for choosing tools and options when you recover data. narration.text: A few more concise reminders: selective restoration using --table or --schema lets you recover only what you need, which is useful for single-table corruption or targeted migrations. Use pg_restore -l to list archive contents; editing the output and applying it with --use-list gives you deterministic control. For performance, --jobs enables parallel restores but requires attention to server C P U, memory, and disk input and output. Finally, always verify restored data counts and role/tablespace creation, and rehearse restores on a non-production environment. These practices reduce surprises and give you operational confidence when performing real recoveries.
